statement: Every small [regular category](c:regular-category) $\mathcal{C}$ has a [full and faithful](c:full-and-faithful-functor) functor into a [presheaf](c:presheaf) category $[\mathcal{R}, \mathbf{Set}]$, with $\mathcal{R}$ small, that preserves finite limits and regular epimorphisms. In particular this embedding is a [conservative functor](c:conservative-functor).

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{C}$ is small.
The category $\mathcal{C}$ is [regular](c:regular-category): it has finite limits and coequalizers of kernel pairs, and regular epimorphisms are stable under pullback.

conclusion: There are a small category $\mathcal{R}$ and a full, faithful functor $\mathcal{C} \to [\mathcal{R}, \mathbf{Set}]$ that preserves finite limits and regular epimorphisms.

proofs.name: Evaluation at regular functors
proofs.slogan: Evaluate each object at a large enough small family of regular functors into sets, and show that evaluation is regular, faithful and full.
proofs.scope: An outline of Barr's proof; steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited work. The same functor is exact when $\mathcal{C}$ is an [exact category](c:exact-category), because it preserves kernel pairs and regular epimorphisms.

roles.why: Smallness bounds the family of regular functors needed, so the target is a presheaf category on a small category.
Regularity makes regular functors into sets meaningful and supplies the images that the faithfulness and fullness arguments use.

steps.slogan: Choose a small full subcategory $\mathcal{R}$ of the regular functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$.
steps.detail: A regular functor $F\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ preserves finite limits and [regular epimorphisms](c:is-regular-epi). Because $\mathcal{C}$ is small, a small full subcategory $\mathcal{R}$ of these functors is large enough for the later steps.

steps.slogan: Define the evaluation functor $\mathrm{ev}\colon \mathcal{C} \to [\mathcal{R}, \mathbf{Set}]$.
steps.detail: Send an object $c$ to the functor $F \mapsto F(c)$ and a morphism $f$ to the natural family $F(f)$. Limits and regular epimorphisms in a functor category are computed pointwise, and every $F \in \mathcal{R}$ preserves them, so $\mathrm{ev}$ preserves finite limits and regular epimorphisms.

steps.slogan: Show that the regular functors in $\mathcal{R}$ separate parallel arrows.
steps.detail: Barr adapts Lubkin's argument: for distinct arrows $f, g\colon c \to d$ of $\mathcal{C}$ he constructs a regular functor $F$ into sets with $F(f) \neq F(g)$. Hence $\mathrm{ev}$ is faithful.

steps.slogan: Enlarge $\mathcal{R}$ so that every natural transformation between evaluations comes from an arrow.
steps.detail: Barr adapts Mitchell's proof of the full embedding of abelian categories. For a large enough $\mathcal{R}$, each natural transformation $\mathrm{ev}(c) \to \mathrm{ev}(d)$ equals $\mathrm{ev}(f)$ for an arrow $f\colon c \to d$, unique by faithfulness.

steps.slogan: Combine the three properties of evaluation into the embedding theorem.
steps.detail: The functor $\mathrm{ev}$ preserves finite limits and regular epimorphisms by step 2, is faithful by step 3 and full by step 4. A full and faithful functor reflects isomorphisms, so it is also conservative.

concepts.c:regular-category: The theorem concerns regular categories, where regular functors to sets make sense.
concepts.c:full-and-faithful-functor: Full and faithful is the property that makes evaluation an embedding.
concepts.c:presheaf: The target is a category of set-valued functors on a small category.
concepts.c:conservative-functor: A full and faithful functor reflects isomorphisms, so it is conservative.
concepts.c:exact-category: The same embedding is exact when the source is an exact category.
concepts.c:is-regular-epi: Regular functors are exactly those that also preserve regular epimorphisms.

source.ref: M. Barr, Exact categories, in: Exact Categories and Categories of Sheaves, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 236, Springer, Berlin, 1971, pp. 1-120
source.note: Barr's embedding theorem for regular categories; the steps outline the Lubkin-style family of regular functors and the Mitchell-style fullness argument of that work.

statement: For every [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) $\mathcal{E}$ there are a [complete Boolean algebra](c:complete-boolean-algebra) $B$ and a surjective [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) $\mathrm{Sh}(B) \to \mathcal{E}$. The topos $\mathrm{Sh}(B)$ of sheaves on $B$ is a [Boolean topos](c:boolean-topos).

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{E}$ is a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos): it is equivalent to sheaves on a small site.

conclusion: A surjective geometric morphism from a Boolean topos $\mathrm{Sh}(B)$ to $\mathcal{E}$ exists.

proofs.name: Diaconescu cover and Boolean cover
proofs.slogan: Cover the topos by a localic topos, cover the locale by one with a complete Boolean algebra of opens, and compose.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof in Mac Lane and Moerdijk, chapter IX, section 9; the construction of the Boolean cover of a locale rests on that work. The family of results includes Deligne's completeness theorem for coherent toposes, which is not proved here.

roles.why: A site for $\mathcal{E}$ lets Diaconescu's theorem produce the localic cover.

steps.slogan: Cover $\mathcal{E} = \mathrm{Sh}(\mathcal{C}, J)$ by a localic topos with the Diaconescu cover.
steps.detail: Diaconescu's theorem identifies geometric morphisms into $\mathrm{Sh}(\mathcal{C}, J)$ with flat $J$-continuous functors. The generic such functor gives a locale $X$ and a surjective (open) geometric morphism $\mathrm{Sh}(X) \to \mathcal{E}$.

steps.slogan: Cover the [locale](c:locale) $X$ by a locale whose opens form a complete Boolean algebra.
steps.detail: Mac Lane and Moerdijk construct a surjection of locales $Y \to X$ with $\mathcal{O}(Y) = B$ a complete Boolean algebra. Surjectivity of a locale map means that the frame map $\mathcal{O}(X) \to B$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Compose the two surjections into one surjective geometric morphism.
steps.detail: A surjection of locales induces a surjective geometric morphism $\mathrm{Sh}(B) \to \mathrm{Sh}(X)$. The composite $\mathrm{Sh}(B) \to \mathrm{Sh}(X) \to \mathcal{E}$ is surjective, as a composite of surjections, and $\mathrm{Sh}(B)$ is Boolean because $B$ is a Boolean algebra.

concepts.c:grothendieck-topos: The theorem covers an arbitrary Grothendieck topos, which has a small site.
concepts.c:complete-boolean-algebra: The cover is sheaves on a complete Boolean algebra.
concepts.c:geometric-morphism: The cover is a geometric morphism, and surjectivity is preserved by composition.
concepts.c:boolean-topos: Sheaves on a Boolean algebra form a Boolean topos, which satisfies classical logic.
concepts.c:locale: The intermediate object is a locale with a surjective localic cover.

source.ref: S. Mac Lane and I. Moerdijk, Sheaves in Geometry and Logic: A First Introduction to Topos Theory, Springer, New York, 1992, chapter IX, section 9 (The Diaconescu cover and Barr's theorem)
source.note: Barr's theorem; the steps follow that section: the Diaconescu cover by a localic topos, then a Boolean cover of the locale.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonsingular projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) over the field $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of [algebraic numbers](c:algebraic-number). Then there is a nonconstant morphism $\beta\colon X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ that is unramified outside $\{0, 1, \infty\}$. So the compact [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) of $X$ is a [branched covering](c:branched-covering) of the sphere branched over three points.

hypotheses.text: The curve $X$ is nonsingular and projective, and defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

conclusion: A nonconstant morphism $\beta\colon X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ has all its critical values in $\{0, 1, \infty\}$.

proofs.name: Belyi's construction
proofs.slogan: Take any function on the curve, make its critical values rational with minimal polynomials, then push them to $0$, $1$, $\infty$ with explicit polynomials.
proofs.scope: The theorem as stated, in the direction from $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ to the three-point map. The converse, that a curve with such a map is defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, is due to Weil and is not proved here.

roles.why: Because $X$ lives over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, a function on it has algebraic critical values.

steps.slogan: Choose a nonconstant function $f$ on $X$ and note that its critical values are algebraic.
steps.detail: Take any nonconstant $f \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$. It is a finite separable map $X \to \mathbb{P}^1$, so it has finitely many ramification points. These are closed points of a curve over the algebraically closed field $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, so their images, the critical values, lie in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cup \{\infty\}$.

steps.slogan: Track the critical values of $g \circ f$ for a rational function $g$.
steps.detail: Ramification indices multiply: $e_{g \circ f}(x) = e_f(x)\, e_g(f(x))$. So the critical values of $g \circ f$ are the images under $g$ of the critical values of $f$, together with the critical values of $g$.

steps.slogan: Compose with minimal polynomials until all finite critical values are rational.
steps.detail: Let $m \ge 2$ be the largest degree over $\mathbb{Q}$ of a finite critical value, let $a$ have degree $m$, and let $P \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be its [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial). By step 2 the new values are $P(b)$ for old values $b$, the values of $P$ at roots of $P'$ (degree below $m$), and $\infty$. As $P(a) = 0$ and $P(b) \in \mathbb{Q}(b)$, the number of values of degree $m$ drops.

steps.slogan: Compose with a Belyi polynomial to remove one critical value from $(0, 1)$.
steps.detail: An affine map over $\mathbb{Q}$ puts the finite critical values into $[0, 1]$, with the extreme two at $0$ and $1$. For a value $c = m/(m+n)$ in $(0, 1)$ take $\varphi(x) = \frac{(m+n)^{m+n}}{m^m n^n} x^m (1-x)^n$. Its critical values are $0$, $1$ and $\infty$, it maps $[0, 1]$ into $[0, 1]$ and sends $c$ to $1$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the composition until the only critical values are $0$, $1$ and $\infty$.
steps.detail: Composing with $\varphi$ sends $c$ to $1$ and every other critical value in $(0, 1)$ to a rational number in $[0, 1]$, while $0$ and $1$ go to $0$. So the number of critical values in $(0, 1)$ drops by at least one each time. After finitely many passes the composite $\beta$ has critical values in $\{0, 1, \infty\}$.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The curve over the algebraic numbers is the object that receives the Belyi map.
concepts.c:algebraic-number: Critical values of a function over the algebraic numbers are algebraic.
concepts.c:riemann-surface: The theorem restates the result for the compact Riemann surface of the curve.
concepts.c:branched-covering: The Belyi map is a branched covering of the sphere with three branch points.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: Minimal polynomials over the rationals lower the degree of the critical values.

source.note: Belyi's proof, G. V. Belyi, On Galois extensions of a maximal cyclotomic field, Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 43 (1979), 267-276.

statement: A unit-mass particle moves under an attractive [central force](c:central-force) of magnitude $f(r) > 0$, with $f$ smooth on $(0, \infty)$ and a stable circular orbit at every radius. If every bounded orbit is closed, then $f(r) = kr$ or $f(r) = k/r^2$ for some $k > 0$. For these two laws every bounded orbit is an ellipse.

hypotheses.text: The force is [central](c:central-force) and attractive, of magnitude $f(r) > 0$ at distance $r$, with $f$ smooth on $(0, \infty)$.
Every radius $r > 0$ carries a stable circular orbit, that is $3f(r) + r f'(r) > 0$.
Every bounded orbit with nonzero angular momentum is closed.

conclusion: The force law is $f(r) = kr$ (Hooke) or $f(r) = k/r^2$ (Kepler) with $k > 0$.

proofs.name: Apsidal angle of near-circular and extreme orbits
proofs.slogan: Closed orbits need a rational apsidal angle, so near-circular orbits force a power law, and two limiting orbits pick out the exponents $1$ and $-2$.
proofs.scope: The force law, in the setting of the hypotheses; the sign convention is that $f > 0$ points to the centre. The proof follows Goldstein and Arnold, with the limits of the apsidal angle computed in the steps.

roles.why: The central force conserves angular momentum and energy, which reduces the motion to the radial equation.
Stable circular orbits at every radius make the near-circular orbits exist, and give $\beta^2 > 0$.
Closed orbits force the apsidal angle to be a rational multiple of $\pi$, at every radius and in the limiting regimes.

steps.slogan: Express closure of an orbit through its [apsidal angle](c:apsidal-angle).
steps.detail: Let $V' = f$, with angular momentum $L \neq 0$ and energy $E$. A bounded orbit swings between two turning radii, and the angle swept between consecutive turning points is $\Phi(E, L) = \int L\, dr \big/ \bigl(r^2 \sqrt{2(E - V) - L^2/r^2}\bigr)$, continuous in $E$ and $L$. The orbit is closed exactly when $\Phi / \pi$ is rational.

steps.slogan: Compute the apsidal angle of nearly circular orbits.
steps.detail: A circular orbit of radius $r_0$ has $f(r_0) = L^2/r_0^3$. Small radial oscillations have frequency squared $f' + 3f/r_0$, and the angular speed is $\sqrt{f/r_0}$. So $\Phi \to \pi/\beta(r_0)$ as the orbit tends to the circle, where $\beta^2 = 3 + r_0 f'(r_0)/f(r_0) > 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\beta$ is constant and rational, and that $f$ is a power law.
steps.detail: At fixed $r_0$ the nearly circular orbits are closed, so $\Phi/\pi$ is rational and continuous in $E$, hence constant, equal to its limit $1/\beta(r_0)$. So $\beta(r_0) \in \mathbb{Q}$, and $\beta$ is continuous in $r_0$, hence constant. Integrating $r f'/f = \beta^2 - 3$ gives $f = k r^{\beta^2 - 3}$.

steps.slogan: Let the angular momentum tend to zero to force $\beta = 2$ when $\beta^2 > 2$.
steps.detail: Then $V = k r^{\beta^2-2}/(\beta^2 - 2)$ and every orbit is bounded. At fixed $E$, $\Phi(E, L)$ is continuous in $L$ with values in $\pi\mathbb{Q}$, so it is constant. It tends to $\pi/\beta$ near the circular orbit, and to $\pi/2$ as $L \to 0$, when the orbit passes close to the centre. So $\beta = 2$ and $f = kr$.

steps.slogan: Let the energy tend to zero to force $\beta = 1$ when $\beta^2 < 2$.
steps.detail: Then $V = -k' r^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha = 2 - \beta^2 \in (0, 2)$. At fixed $L$, $\Phi$ is constant for $E$ between the circular energy and $0$. It tends to $\pi/\beta$ at the circular energy and, by the substitution $t = (r_{\min}/r)^{(2-\alpha)/2}$, to $\pi/(2-\alpha) = \pi/\beta^2$ as $E \to 0^-$. So $\beta^2 = \beta$, $\beta = 1$ and $f = k/r^2$.

steps.slogan: Exclude $\beta^2 = 2$ and check that both remaining laws give closed orbits.
steps.detail: Since $\beta$ is rational, $\beta^2 \neq 2$. So $\beta = 2$ (Hooke) or $\beta = 1$ (Kepler). Both laws integrate to ellipses: the Hooke orbit is $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a}\cos\omega t + \mathbf{b}\sin\omega t$, and a bounded Kepler orbit is a conic of eccentricity below $1$.

concepts.c:central-force: The force depends only on the distance, so angular momentum is conserved.
concepts.c:apsidal-angle: Closure of an orbit is equivalent to rationality of its apsidal angle over $\pi$.

source.note: The classical near-circular and limiting-orbit argument: H. Goldstein, C. Poole and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, 3rd edition, section 3.6 and appendix A; V. I. Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, section 8.

new_concepts.name: central force
new_concepts.reminder: A central force on a point mass points along the line to a fixed centre and depends only on the distance.
new_concepts.definition: A force $\mathbf{F}$ on a particle at position $\mathbf{r}$ is central when $\mathbf{F} = F(r)\,\mathbf{r}/r$ with $r = |\mathbf{r}|$. It conserves angular momentum about the centre.

new_concepts.name: apsidal angle
new_concepts.reminder: The apsidal angle is the angle swept about the centre between two consecutive turning points of the radius.
new_concepts.definition: For a bounded orbit in a central force, the radius oscillates between a minimum and a maximum. The apsidal angle is the change of the polar angle from one to the next.

statement: A load is fed by $N$ conductors with currents $i_1, \dots, i_N$ that obey [Kirchhoff's current law](c:kirchhoff-current-law) $\sum_k i_k = 0$. Then its total power is $\sum_{k=1}^{N-1} (v_k - v_N)\, i_k$, the sum of the readings of $N - 1$ [wattmeters](c:wattmeter) that share conductor $N$ as voltage reference. Fewer than $N - 1$ wattmeters fail for some load.

hypotheses.text: The currents satisfy $\sum_{k=1}^N i_k = 0$ at every instant.
The power drawn by the load is $p = \sum_{k=1}^N v_k i_k$, where $v_k$ is the potential of conductor $k$ relative to one fixed reference point.
A [wattmeter](c:wattmeter) has its current coil in one conductor and reads the average of the current times the voltage across its voltage coil.

conclusion: Wattmeters in conductors $1, \dots, N-1$ with voltage coils to conductor $N$ read the total power, and $N - 2$ wattmeters cannot do so for every load.

proofs.name: Shift of the voltage reference
proofs.slogan: Current conservation lets the reference potential move to conductor $N$, which removes one term, and a load between two unmetered conductors shows that fewer meters fail.
proofs.scope: Instantaneous power, so the average power and the energy follow by integration over time. The minimum $N - 1$ is proved for loads connected between arbitrary pairs of conductors.

roles.why: The zero sum of currents makes the power independent of the voltage reference.
The sum $\sum v_k i_k$ is the quantity that the shift and the dropped term rewrite.
A meter has one current coil, so each meter reads one term, and $N - 2$ meters leave two conductors unmetered.

steps.slogan: Shift every potential so that conductor $N$ becomes the reference point.
steps.detail: Replace each $v_k$ by $v_k - c$ with a constant $c$. The power changes by $-c \sum_k i_k$, which is zero by [Kirchhoff's current law](c:kirchhoff-current-law). So $p$ does not depend on the reference, and we may take $c = v_N$.

steps.slogan: Drop the term of conductor $N$ and read the remaining terms as wattmeter readings.
steps.detail: With $c = v_N$ the term of conductor $N$ is $(v_N - v_N)\, i_N = 0$. So $p = \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} (v_k - v_N)\, i_k$. Term $k$ is the reading of a [wattmeter](c:wattmeter) with its current coil in conductor $k$ and its voltage coil from $k$ to $N$.

steps.slogan: Show that $N - 2$ wattmeters miss a load between two unmetered conductors.
steps.detail: With $N - 2$ meters, each with one current coil, at least two conductors $j \neq l$ carry no current coil. Connect only a resistor $R$ between $j$ and $l$. Every current coil carries zero current, so every reading is zero, yet the load takes the power $R i^2 > 0$.

steps.slogan: State the minimum: $N - 1$ wattmeters suffice and $N - 2$ do not.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives the total power from $N - 1$ meters for every load. Step 3 gives a load that $N - 2$ meters read as zero, so the number $N - 1$ is the minimum for a general system.

concepts.c:kirchhoff-current-law: Zero total current is what lets the voltage reference be moved freely.
concepts.c:wattmeter: Each wattmeter reading is one term of the power sum.

source.note: The standard argument for Blondel's theorem (A. Blondel, 1893): shift the voltage reference by Kirchhoff's current law; the lower bound is a one-resistor counterexample.

new_concepts.name: Kirchhoff's current law
new_concepts.reminder: The signed currents flowing into a node, or through the terminals of a lumped load, add up to zero at every instant.
new_concepts.definition: At every instant the sum of the currents into a node, or into a lumped network through its terminals, is zero, because charge does not accumulate there.

new_concepts.name: wattmeter
new_concepts.reminder: A wattmeter reads the time average of the product of the current in one conductor and a voltage.
new_concepts.definition: A wattmeter has a current coil in series with one conductor and a voltage coil across two chosen points. Its reading is the average of the current times the voltage.

statement: Let $N$ classical charged particles in a bounded region be in the [canonical ensemble](c:canonical-ensemble) at temperature $T$, with [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H = \sum_j |\mathbf{p}_j - q_j \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}_j)|^2 / 2m_j + U(\mathbf{r})$. Then the [partition function](c:partition-function) does not depend on the applied field $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$, so the thermal average [magnetization](c:magnetization) is zero.

hypotheses.text: The [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) is $H = \sum_j |\mathbf{p}_j - q_j \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}_j)|^2 / 2m_j + U(\mathbf{r})$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is a vector potential of $\mathbf{B}$ and $U$ does not depend on $\mathbf{p}$ or $\mathbf{A}$.
The positions range over a bounded region $\Omega^N$, with the walls part of $U$, and the momenta range over all of $\mathbb{R}^{3N}$.
The system is in the [canonical ensemble](c:canonical-ensemble): the phase-space density is proportional to the [Boltzmann weight](c:boltzmann-distribution) $e^{-H/k_B T}$, and $U$ is bounded below.

conclusion: The partition function satisfies $Z(\mathbf{B}) = Z(0)$ for every field, so the free energy $F = -k_B T \ln Z$ does not depend on $B$ and $M = -\partial F/\partial B = 0$.

proofs.name: Shift of the momenta
proofs.slogan: Shift each momentum by the vector potential at fixed positions, so that the field disappears from the partition function.
proofs.scope: A finite classical system in thermal equilibrium; the average magnetic moment is $-\partial F/\partial B$. The proof does not cover quantum systems, which can be magnetic.

roles.why: Minimal coupling puts $\mathbf{A}$ only in the combination $\mathbf{p} - q\mathbf{A}$, which a shift of $\mathbf{p}$ removes.
Momenta range over all of $\mathbb{R}^{3N}$, so the shift maps momentum space onto itself, and the bounded positions keep the integral finite.
The Boltzmann weight turns the Hamiltonian into the partition function and its free energy.

steps.slogan: Write the [partition function](c:partition-function) as an integral over phase space.
steps.detail: $Z(\mathbf{B}) = \int_{\Omega^N} d^{3N}r \int_{\mathbb{R}^{3N}} d^{3N}p\; e^{-H/k_B T}$, up to constant factors. The integrand is positive, so Tonelli's theorem allows any order of integration.

steps.slogan: Shift each momentum by $q_j \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}_j)$ at fixed positions.
steps.detail: Fix $\mathbf{r} \in \Omega^N$ and put $\mathbf{p}'_j = \mathbf{p}_j - q_j \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}_j)$. This is a translation of $\mathbb{R}^{3N}$, so $d^{3N}p' = d^{3N}p$ and momentum space maps onto itself. The kinetic energy becomes $\sum_j |\mathbf{p}'_j|^2/2m_j$, which contains no $\mathbf{A}$.

steps.slogan: Factor the integral to show that $Z$ does not depend on $\mathbf{A}$.
steps.detail: After the shift, $Z = \int_{\Omega^N} e^{-U/k_B T}\, d^{3N}r \cdot \prod_j \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} e^{-|\mathbf{p}'|^2/2m_j k_B T}\, d^3p'$. Neither factor contains $\mathbf{A}$, so $Z(\mathbf{B}) = Z(0)$ for every field.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the free energy to get zero [magnetization](c:magnetization).
steps.detail: The thermal average of the magnetic moment $-\partial H/\partial B$ equals $-\partial F/\partial B = k_B T\, \partial \ln Z/\partial B$ with $F = -k_B T \ln Z$. This is zero because $Z$ is constant in $B$.

concepts.c:canonical-ensemble: The equilibrium state is the canonical ensemble with the Boltzmann weight.
concepts.c:hamiltonian: The Hamiltonian carries the field only through $\mathbf{p} - q\mathbf{A}$.
concepts.c:partition-function: The partition function generates the free energy and so the magnetization.
concepts.c:magnetization: The magnetization is the derivative of the free energy with respect to the field.
concepts.c:boltzmann-distribution: The Boltzmann weight fixes the integrand of the partition function.

source.note: The classical shift-of-momenta argument of N. Bohr (doctoral thesis, Copenhagen, 1911) and H. J. van Leeuwen, Journal de Physique et le Radium 2 (1921), 361-377.

new_concepts.name: magnetization
new_concepts.reminder: Magnetization is the thermal average magnetic moment of a sample, equal to minus the derivative of the free energy with respect to the field.
new_concepts.definition: The magnetization $M$ of a system in a field $B$ is the thermal average of its magnetic moment $-\partial H/\partial B$. For the free energy $F$ it equals $-\partial F/\partial B$.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth projective varieties over a field, with $X$ having [ample canonical bundle](c:ample-canonical-bundle) or ample anticanonical bundle. If the bounded [derived categories](c:derived-category) of coherent sheaves of $X$ and $Y$ are equivalent as triangulated categories, then $X \cong Y$.

hypotheses.text: The varieties $X$ and $Y$ are smooth [projective varieties](c:projective-variety) over a field $k$.
The canonical bundle $\omega_X$ or its inverse $\omega_X^{-1}$ is ample.
There is an equivalence of triangulated categories $D^b(\mathrm{Coh}\, X) \simeq D^b(\mathrm{Coh}\, Y)$.

conclusion: The varieties $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic as schemes.

proofs.name: Point objects, invertible objects and the canonical ring
proofs.slogan: Recover points, line bundles and the canonical ring of $X$ from the derived category and the Serre functor, then transport them to $Y$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Bondal and Orlov's proof; steps 2, 3 and 5 rest on the cited paper. The same paper also computes the group of autoequivalences, which is not proved here.

roles.why: Smoothness and projectivity give Serre duality, hence a Serre functor on the derived category.
Ampleness of $\omega_X^{\pm 1}$ makes point objects shifted skyscrapers and lets the canonical ring rebuild $X$.
An equivalence preserves the Serre functor and all categorical characterizations, which moves the construction to $Y$.

steps.slogan: Recover the [Serre functor](c:serre-functor) from the triangulated category alone.
steps.detail: By Serre duality, $S_X = -\otimes \omega_X[n]$ with $n = \dim X$ is a Serre functor of $D^b(X)$. A Serre functor is unique up to isomorphism, so every equivalence of triangulated categories commutes with it.

steps.slogan: Characterize point objects by conditions on the Serre functor and the Hom groups.
steps.detail: Call $P$ a point object if $S(P) \cong P[n]$, $\mathrm{Hom}^{<0}(P, P) = 0$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(P, P)$ is a field. When $\omega_X$ or $\omega_X^{-1}$ is ample, these are exactly the shifts $k(x)[r]$ of skyscraper sheaves, so the closed points are recovered.

steps.slogan: Characterize invertible objects through their Hom groups with point objects.
steps.detail: Call $L$ invertible if, for every point object $P$, exactly one $\mathrm{Hom}^i(L, P)$ is nonzero and it is one-dimensional over $\mathrm{Hom}(P, P)$. These are exactly the shifted line bundles $\mathcal{L}[m]$.

steps.slogan: Build the graded algebra $\bigoplus_i \mathrm{Hom}(L, S^i L[-in])$ from the category.
steps.detail: For $L = \mathcal{L}$ the summand is $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{L} \otimes \omega_X^{i}) = H^0(X, \omega_X^i)$. Since $\omega_X$, or $\omega_X^{-1}$ with $S^{-1}$, is ample, $X \cong \mathrm{Proj} \bigoplus_{i \ge 0} H^0(X, \omega_X^{\pm i})$.

steps.slogan: Transport the construction along the equivalence to identify $Y$ with $X$.
steps.detail: An equivalence $D^b(X) \to D^b(Y)$ preserves $S$, point objects and invertible objects. So it carries the invertible objects above to a sequence in $D^b(Y)$ with the same graded algebra, and Bondal and Orlov show by the ample-sequence criterion that it is an ample sequence of line bundles on $Y$ up to shifts. Hence $Y \cong \mathrm{Proj}$ of the same ring, and $Y \cong X$.

concepts.c:ample-canonical-bundle: Ampleness of the canonical or anticanonical bundle lets the canonical ring rebuild the variety.
concepts.c:derived-category: The hypothesis and all intrinsic structure live in the derived category.
concepts.c:projective-variety: Projective varieties are recovered as Proj of a graded ring.
concepts.c:serre-functor: The Serre functor is intrinsic to the category and encodes the canonical bundle.

source.ref: A. Bondal and D. Orlov, Reconstruction of a variety from the derived category and groups of autoequivalences, Compositio Mathematica 125 (2001), 327-344
source.note: Bondal and Orlov characterize point objects, invertible objects and the Zariski topology cohomologically, using ample sequences in the abelian category.

statement: Let $G^*$ be the [HNN extension](c:hnn-extension) $\langle G, t \mid t a t^{-1} = \varphi(a),\ a \in A \rangle$ of a group $G$ along an isomorphism $\varphi\colon A \to B$ of subgroups. Let $g_0 t^{\epsilon_1} g_1 \cdots t^{\epsilon_n} g_n$ with $g_i \in G$ and $\epsilon_i = \pm 1$ be a [reduced word](c:reduced-word). If it represents an element of $G$, then $n = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G^*$ is the [HNN extension](c:hnn-extension) of $G$ along $\varphi\colon A \to B$, so $t a = \varphi(a) t$ for $a \in A$.
The word is [reduced](c:reduced-word): no subword $t^{\epsilon} g\, t^{-\epsilon}$ has $g \in A$ when $\epsilon = 1$ or $g \in B$ when $\epsilon = -1$.
The word represents an element of the base group $G$, that is of the image of $G$ in $G^*$.

conclusion: The word has no letter $t^{\pm 1}$, that is $n = 0$.

proofs.name: Action on normal words
proofs.slogan: Let the HNN extension act on normal words, so that every element has one normal form, then compare a reduced word with the word of its value in $G$.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, including $n = 0$ and the one-letter word. A reduced word that represents $1$ is the special case.

roles.why: The relation $t a = \varphi(a) t$ is what lets $t$ act consistently on normal words.
Absence of pinches keeps the rewriting into a normal word free of cancellation, so the signs survive.
The word has the same value as a word without $t$, which is what the comparison uses.

steps.slogan: Choose [representatives](c:coset-representatives) of the right cosets of $A$ and of $B$ in $G$.
steps.detail: Pick sets $T_1$ and $T_{-1}$ that hold exactly one element of each right coset of $A$, respectively $B$, with $1$ for the trivial coset. A normal word is $g_0 t^{\epsilon_1} r_1 \cdots t^{\epsilon_n} r_n$ with $r_i \in T_{\epsilon_i}$ and no pinch.

steps.slogan: Let $G$ and $t$ act on the [normal words](c:normal-form) so that the relation $t a = \varphi(a) t$ holds.
steps.detail: The group $G$ acts by multiplying the head $g_0$. For $t^{\epsilon}$, write $g_0 = a r$ with $a \in A$ or $B$ and $r$ a representative. If the word starts with $t^{-\epsilon}$ and $r = 1$, cancel the pair and apply $\varphi^{\pm 1}$ to $a$; otherwise move $\varphi^{\pm 1}(a)$ to the head and insert $t^{\epsilon} r$. These maps satisfy the relation, so the HNN extension acts.

steps.slogan: Show that the product map from normal words to $G^*$ is injective.
steps.detail: Under the [group action](c:group-action), an element $g \in G^*$ sends the empty word to a normal word $g \cdot \varnothing$, and induction on a word for $g$ shows that its product is $g$. The product of a normal word, acting on the empty word, returns that word, by induction on its length. So the product map is a bijection.

steps.slogan: Rewrite every reduced word as a normal word with the same product and signs.
steps.detail: Work from the right: write $g_i = a\, r_i$ with $a \in A$ or $B$ and $r_i$ a representative, and push $a$ left through $t^{\epsilon_i}$ by $t a = \varphi(a) t$. This changes only the group letters, so the signs $\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_n$ stay. A new pinch would force an original letter $g_i$ into $A$ or $B$, which reducedness excludes.

steps.slogan: Compare the given word with the one-letter word $g$ to get $n = 0$.
steps.detail: Let the word represent $g \in G$. The word $g$ with no $t$ is also reduced and has the same product. Rewrite both as normal words; the products agree, so the normal words are equal. Rewriting kept the signs, so the given word has the signs of $g$, which are none. Hence $n = 0$.

concepts.c:hnn-extension: The lemma describes words in an HNN extension and its relation $ta = \varphi(a)t$.
concepts.c:reduced-word: Reducedness, the absence of pinches, is the hypothesis that blocks cancellation.
concepts.c:coset-representatives: Coset representatives define the normal form of each letter.
concepts.c:normal-form: Normal words give each element of the extension a unique form.
concepts.c:group-action: The action on normal words shows that normal forms are unique.

source.note: mathlib lets the extension act on NormalWord (unitsSMul), proves NormalWord.prod_injective from prod_smul_empty, rewrites reduced words with exists_normalWord_prod_eq, and concludes with map_fst_eq_and_of_prod_eq.

statement: Let a unitary two-dimensional quantum field theory with running couplings be invariant under translations and rotations, with a conserved symmetric stress tensor. Then a function $C$ of the couplings decreases along the [renormalization group](c:renormalization-group) flow toward the infrared and is stationary only at scale-invariant points. There it equals the [central charge](c:central-charge) $c$ of the [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory).

hypotheses.text: The theory is unitary, in the form of [reflection positivity](c:reflection-positivity) of its correlators.
The theory is invariant under translations and rotations of the plane, that is under [Lorentz invariance](c:lorentz-invariance) after continuation to real time.
A symmetric stress tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ exists and is conserved, $\partial^\mu T_{\mu\nu} = 0$, along the whole flow.

conclusion: For $t = \ln(z\bar z)$ the function $C = 2F - G - \tfrac38 H$ of the stress-tensor correlators obeys $\dot C = -\tfrac34 H \le 0$, is stationary only where the trace $\Theta$ vanishes, and equals $c$ there.

proofs.name: Zamolodchikov's function
proofs.slogan: Write the stress-tensor correlators with three scalar functions, use conservation to relate them, and build $C$ so that its derivative is minus a positive correlator.
proofs.scope: Euclidean plane, with the normalization of $T$ in which a fixed point has $\langle T(z)T(0)\rangle = c/2z^4$. The proof assumes the stated axioms and does not construct the theory.

roles.why: Rotation and translation invariance fix the tensor structure of the two-point functions.
Conservation of $T_{\mu\nu}$ gives the differential equations that relate $F$, $G$ and $H$.
[Reflection positivity](c:reflection-positivity) makes the trace two-point function $H$ nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the stress tensor two-point functions by three scalar functions.
steps.detail: Use complex coordinates, with $T = T_{zz}$, $\Theta = T^\mu{}_\mu$ the trace and $\bar T$ the conjugate component. Invariance gives $\langle T(z)T(0)\rangle = F/z^4$, $\langle T(z)\Theta(0)\rangle = G/(z^3 \bar z)$ and $\langle \Theta(z)\Theta(0)\rangle = H/(z^2 \bar z^2)$. The functions $F$, $G$, $H$ depend on $t = \ln(z\bar z)$ and on the running couplings.

steps.slogan: Turn conservation of the stress tensor into two differential equations for $F$, $G$ and $H$.
steps.detail: Conservation reads $\partial_{\bar z} T + \tfrac14 \partial_z \Theta = 0$. Taking its correlators with $T(0)$ and $\Theta(0)$ gives $\dot F + \tfrac14(\dot G - 3G) = 0$ and $\dot G - G + \tfrac14(\dot H - 2H) = 0$, with the dot for $d/dt$.

steps.slogan: Form $C = 2F - G - \tfrac38 H$ and compute its derivative.
steps.detail: The equations give $\dot F = -\tfrac14(\dot G - 3G)$ and $\dot G = G - \tfrac14 \dot H + \tfrac12 H$. Then $\dot C = 2\dot F - \dot G - \tfrac38 \dot H$, and after substitution all terms in $G$ and $\dot H$ cancel, leaving $\dot C = -\tfrac34 H$.

steps.slogan: Use [reflection positivity](c:reflection-positivity) to show $H \ge 0$, so $C$ decreases.
steps.detail: $H = |z|^4 \langle \Theta(z)\Theta(0)\rangle$ is the norm of a state created by $\Theta$, so reflection positivity gives $H \ge 0$. Hence $\dot C \le 0$, and $C$ decreases as the distance grows, toward the infrared. If $H = 0$, the state is zero, so $\Theta = 0$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $C$ at a point where it is stationary.
steps.detail: Where $\dot C = 0$ we have $\Theta = 0$, so the theory is scale invariant and $G = H = 0$. The two-point function of $T$ is $F/z^4$, and the central charge of the [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) is defined by $F = c/2$. Hence $C = 2F = c$.

concepts.c:renormalization-group: The function $C$ is monotone along the renormalization group flow.
concepts.c:central-charge: The value of $C$ at a fixed point is the central charge.
concepts.c:conformal-field-theory: Scale-invariant fixed points are conformal field theories with a central charge.
concepts.c:reflection-positivity: Reflection positivity is the form of unitarity that gives $H \ge 0$.
concepts.c:lorentz-invariance: Rotation and translation symmetry fix the form of the correlators.

source.note: Zamolodchikov's argument, A. B. Zamolodchikov, Irreversibility of the flux of the renormalization group in a 2D field theory, JETP Letters 43 (1986), 730-732.

statement: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m}, k)$ be a Noetherian [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring). If $R$ contains a field, then $R \cong k[[x_1, \dots, x_n]]/I$. Otherwise $R \cong \Lambda[[x_1, \dots, x_n]]/I$, where $\Lambda$ is a Cohen ring: a complete [discrete valuation ring](c:discrete-valuation-ring) with maximal ideal $(p)$ and residue field $k$, for $p = \operatorname{char} k$. Here $[[\cdot]]$ is a [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) ring.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ and residue field $k$.
The ring $R$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring), so $\mathfrak{m}$ is finitely generated.
The ring $R$ is complete in the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology.

conclusion: The ring $R$ is a quotient of $\Lambda[[x_1, \dots, x_n]]$, with $\Lambda = k$ if $R$ contains a field and $\Lambda$ a Cohen ring otherwise.

proofs.name: Coefficient ring and power series map
proofs.slogan: Find a coefficient field or Cohen ring in $R$, map a power series ring onto $R$ by sending variables to generators of $\mathfrak{m}$, and take the kernel.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, in the two cases that $R$ contains a field or not. The case $n = 0$ is a field or a quotient of a Cohen ring.

roles.why: The residue field $k$ and its characteristic decide whether the coefficient ring is a field or a Cohen ring.
Finite generation of $\mathfrak{m}$ gives finitely many variables.
[Completeness](c:complete-local-ring) makes power series in the generators converge and makes the map onto.

steps.slogan: Find a coefficient field or a Cohen ring inside $R$.
steps.detail: If $R$ contains a field, Zorn's lemma gives a maximal subfield $K \subseteq R$. Hensel's lemma, and a $p$-basis argument when $\operatorname{char} k = p$, show that $K \to k$ is onto, so $K$ is a coefficient field. If not, $p = \operatorname{char} k > 0$, and a Cohen ring with residue field $k$ lifts into $R$ by completeness.

steps.slogan: Send the variables to generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ to define a map from a power series ring.
steps.detail: As $R$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak{m} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$. Define $\Lambda[[X_1, \dots, X_n]] \to R$ by $X_i \mapsto x_i$ on the coefficient ring $\Lambda$ of step 1. It is well defined because every [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) in the $x_i$ converges in the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology of $R$.

steps.slogan: Show that the map from the power series ring to $R$ is surjective.
steps.detail: Modulo $\mathfrak{m}$ the map is onto $k$, since $\Lambda \to k$ is onto. Every element of $\mathfrak{m}^j$ is a combination of degree $j$ monomials in the $x_i$, so successive approximation by power series, with completeness, reaches every element of $R$. This is the complete form of Nakayama's lemma.

steps.slogan: Present $R$ as the quotient of the power series ring by the kernel.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be the kernel of the surjection, so $R \cong \Lambda[[X_1, \dots, X_n]]/I$. When $R$ contains a field, $\Lambda$ is a field isomorphic to $k$; otherwise $\Lambda$ is a Cohen ring, a complete [discrete valuation ring](c:discrete-valuation-ring) with maximal ideal $(p)$.

concepts.c:complete-local-ring: Completeness makes power series converge and gives surjectivity of the map.
concepts.c:noetherian-ring: The Noetherian hypothesis gives finitely many generators of the maximal ideal.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The ring $R$ is presented as a quotient of a formal power series ring.
concepts.c:discrete-valuation-ring: A Cohen ring is a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $p$.

source.note: Stacks Project, Algebra, Theorem 10.160.8 (Cohen structure theorem): coefficient ring, map from a power series ring, and surjectivity.

statement: A [cube](c:cube) cannot be cut into finitely many cubes, at least two, with faces parallel to those of the big cube and with pairwise different side lengths.

hypotheses.text: A cube $Q$ is the union of $m \ge 2$ cubes $Q_1, \dots, Q_m$ with disjoint interiors and faces parallel to those of $Q$.
The side lengths of $Q_1, \dots, Q_m$ are pairwise different.

conclusion: No dissection of a cube into finitely many cubes of pairwise different sizes exists.

proofs.name: Littlewood's descent
proofs.slogan: The smallest cube on the bottom face sits in a well, so smaller different cubes tile its top face, and the argument repeats forever.
proofs.scope: Dissections into at least two cubes with parallel faces. A dissection into one cube is the trivial case $Q_1 = Q$, excluded by $m \ge 2$.

roles.why: The cubes tile the bottom face and the top face of each cube resting on it, and $m \ge 2$ puts those faces below the top of $Q$.
Distinct sides make the smallest square unique and make every cube on its top face strictly smaller.

steps.slogan: Cut the bottom face of $Q$ into the squares of the cubes that rest on it.
steps.detail: No $Q_i$ equals $Q$ because $m \ge 2$, so the cubes that touch the bottom face have bottoms that tile it by at least two [squares](c:square). Their sides are pairwise different by the second hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Show that the smallest square of such a tiling does not touch the boundary.
steps.detail: Let $S$, of side $s$, be the smallest square, and suppose it touches a side. The squares beside $S$ along that side are larger, so above $S$ there is a gap of width exactly $s$ between two walls taller than $S$; the border may be one wall. The squares resting on $S$ fill this gap, so their sides are at most $s$ and not $s$, against minimality of $s$.

steps.slogan: Show that the cubes on top of the smallest bottom cube tile its top face by smaller squares.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the smallest bottom cube, of side $s$; its top lies below the top of $Q$. By step 2 larger, taller cubes surround it, so its top face lies at the bottom of a well. The cubes resting on that face stay in its footprint and tile it; none has side $s$, so all are smaller and there are at least two.

steps.slogan: Repeat the argument on the top face to get an infinite decreasing chain of cubes.
steps.detail: The top face of $S$ is a square tiled by at least two squares with different sides below $s$. Steps 2 and 3 apply to it: its smallest square is the bottom of a cube $S'$ of side $s' < s$, which again has a well on top. This gives different cubes with sides $s > s' > s'' > \cdots$, but only $m$ cubes exist, a contradiction.

concepts.c:cube: The theorem concerns a cube and the cubes that dissect it.
concepts.c:square: The faces of the cubes tile as squares, and the smallest square is the key.

source.note: The descent proof credited to J. E. Littlewood in the name of the catalog record, with the smallest-square lemma proved in full.

statement: Every closed [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$ with finite [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is a [spherical space form](c:spherical-space-form): $M \cong S^3/\Gamma$ for a finite group $\Gamma \subset O(4)$ that acts freely on $S^3$. Equivalently, $M$ carries a metric of constant sectional curvature $1$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a closed connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold).
The [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(M)$ is finite.

conclusion: The manifold $M$ is diffeomorphic to $S^3/\Gamma$ for a finite group $\Gamma$ acting freely on $S^3$.

proofs.name: Ricci flow with surgery
proofs.slogan: Run Ricci flow with surgery from any metric, show it dies in finite time because $\pi_1$ is finite, and rebuild $M$ from the dying pieces.
proofs.scope: An outline for orientable $M$; a closed nonorientable 3-manifold has infinite fundamental group by Epstein, so finiteness forces orientability. Steps 1 to 4 rest on Perelman's work, and the family includes the Poincare conjecture, the case of trivial $\pi_1$.

roles.why: A closed orientable 3-manifold carries a metric and a Ricci flow with surgery that cuts along 2-spheres.
Finite $\pi_1$ makes the flow die in finite time and removes $S^2 \times S^1$ and all but one summand.

steps.slogan: Run [Ricci flow](c:ricci-flow) with surgery from a metric on $M$.
steps.detail: For any metric on a closed orientable 3-manifold, Perelman constructs a Ricci flow with surgery. Its surgeries cut along embedded 2-spheres and discard components, using the canonical neighborhood theorem.

steps.slogan: Show that the flow with surgery becomes extinct in finite time.
steps.detail: A closed 3-manifold with finite $\pi_1$ has no aspherical prime factor. For such $M$, Perelman's finite extinction time argument, with Colding and Minicozzi, shows that the min-max width of 2-sphere sweepouts reaches zero in finite time, so every component disappears.

steps.slogan: Identify the components just before they disappear.
steps.detail: A component about to vanish has the geometry that the canonical neighborhood theorem gives, and it is diffeomorphic to a [spherical space form](c:spherical-space-form) $S^3/\Gamma$, to an $S^2$-bundle over $S^1$, or to $\mathbb{RP}^3 \# \mathbb{RP}^3$.

steps.slogan: Run the surgeries backwards to rebuild $M$ from these pieces.
steps.detail: Each surgery cuts along a 2-sphere, so undoing it forms a [connected sum](c:connected-sum) of two components, or a self connected sum that adds an $S^2$-bundle over $S^1$ as a summand. So $M$ is a connected sum of the final pieces.

steps.slogan: Use finite $\pi_1$ to leave exactly one spherical summand.
steps.detail: The fundamental group of a connected sum is the free product of the groups of the summands. A summand with fibre $S^2$ over $S^1$ gives a factor $\mathbb{Z}$, and two nontrivial factors give an infinite free product. So all but one summand are $S^3$, and $M \cong S^3/\Gamma$.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem classifies closed 3-manifolds with a finiteness condition.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: Finiteness of the fundamental group drives extinction and the final summand count.
concepts.c:spherical-space-form: The result and the pieces of the final stage are spherical space forms.
concepts.c:ricci-flow: Ricci flow with surgery is the engine of the proof.
concepts.c:connected-sum: Reversing surgeries along spheres forms connected sums.

source.ref: G. Perelman, Ricci flow with surgery on three-manifolds, arXiv:math/0303109 (2003), and Finite extinction time for the solutions to the Ricci flow on certain three-manifolds, arXiv:math/0307245 (2003); details in J. Morgan and G. Tian, Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Monographs 3, American Mathematical Society, 2007
source.note: The outline follows Perelman's Ricci flow with surgery and the finite extinction argument, as written out by Morgan and Tian.

Let $(X, Y)$ be bivariate [normal](c:normal-distribution) with means $\mu_x$, $\mu_y 
e 0$ and covariance $\sigma^2 V$ with $V$ known, and let $s^2$ be an independent estimate with $
u s^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_
u$. With $\hat V = s^2 V$ and $t$ the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the [Student's t distribution](c:student-t-distribution) with $
u$ degrees of freedom, the set of $ho_0$ with $(X - ho_0 Y)^2 \le t^2\, \hat V(ho_0)$ is a [confidence interval](c:confidence-interval) for $\mu_x/\mu_y$ of exact level $1 - \alpha$.

hypotheses.text: The pair $(X, Y)$ is bivariate [normal](c:normal-distribution) with mean $(\mu_x, \mu_y)$, $\mu_y \neq 0$, and covariance $\sigma^2 V$ for a known positive definite $V$.
The estimate $s^2$ is independent of $(X, Y)$, and $\nu s^2/\sigma^2$ has the [chi-squared distribution](c:chi-squared-distribution) with $\nu$ degrees of freedom.

conclusion: The set has coverage exactly $1 - \alpha$; for $g = t^2 v_{22}/Y^2 < 1$ it is the interval with ends $\frac{1}{1-g}\bigl[R - \frac{g v_{12}}{v_{22}} \pm \frac{t}{Y}\sqrt{v_{11} - 2Rv_{12} + R^2 v_{22} - g(v_{11} - v_{12}^2/v_{22})}\bigr]$, where $R = X/Y$.

proofs.name: Inversion of a $t$ pivot
proofs.slogan: At the true ratio the combination $X - \rho Y$ has mean zero, which gives a $t$ pivot, and inverting the pivot gives a quadratic inequality in $\rho_0$.
proofs.scope: Here $\hat V(\rho_0) = v_{11} - 2\rho_0 v_{12} + \rho_0^2 v_{22}$ with $v_{ij}$ the entries of $\hat V$. For $g \ge 1$ the set is unbounded: the whole line or the outside of an interval.

roles.why: Normality makes $X - \rho Y$ normal with mean zero at the true $\rho$, and $\mu_y \ne 0$ defines the ratio.
An independent chi-squared estimate of $\sigma^2$ turns the standardized variable into a Student pivot.

steps.slogan: Form the linear combination $X - \rho Y$ at the true ratio $\rho$.
steps.detail: At $\rho = \mu_x/\mu_y$ the mean of $X - \rho Y$ is $\mu_x - \rho \mu_y = 0$. It is [normal](c:normal-distribution) with variance $\sigma^2 (V_{11} - 2\rho V_{12} + \rho^2 V_{22})$, which is positive because $V$ is positive definite.

steps.slogan: Divide by the estimated standard deviation to get a pivot with a Student $t_\nu$ law.
steps.detail:
Put $T(ho) = (X - ho Y)/\sqrt{\hat V(ho)}$. It is a standard normal variable divided by $\sqrt{(
u s^2/\sigma^2)/
u}$, with independent [chi-squared](c:chi-squared-distribution) denominator, so $T(ho) \sim t_
u$ whatever $\sigma$ is.

steps.slogan: Invert the probability statement about the pivot into a confidence set.
steps.detail: By the choice of $t$, $P(|T(\rho)| \le t) = 1 - \alpha$. For each $\rho_0$, $|T(\rho_0)| \le t$ holds exactly when $(X - \rho_0 Y)^2 \le t^2 \hat V(\rho_0)$, so the set contains $\rho$ with probability exactly $1 - \alpha$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the inequality as a quadratic inequality in $\rho_0$.
steps.detail: Expanding gives $(Y^2 - t^2 v_{22})\rho_0^2 - 2(XY - t^2 v_{12})\rho_0 + (X^2 - t^2 v_{11}) \le 0$. Divide by $Y^2$ and write $g = t^2 v_{22}/Y^2$ and $R = X/Y$ to get $(1-g)\rho_0^2 - 2(R - g v_{12}/v_{22})\rho_0 + \dots \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Solve the quadratic with its discriminant to get the interval for $g < 1$.
steps.detail: A quarter of the discriminant is $t^2 Y^2 [v_{11} - 2Rv_{12} + R^2 v_{22} - g(v_{11} - v_{12}^2/v_{22})]$, which is at least $t^2 Y^2 (1-g)(v_{11} - v_{12}^2/v_{22}) > 0$ when $g < 1$. So the solution set is the interval between the two roots, which are the stated ends.

concepts.c:normal-distribution: Normality gives the distribution of the combination $X - \rho Y$.
concepts.c:confidence-interval: The result is a confidence set with exact coverage.
concepts.c:chi-squared-distribution: The chi-squared estimate of the variance gives the Student pivot.
concepts.c:student-t-distribution: The pivot has a Student $t_\nu$ law, which sets the quantile $t$.

source.note: Fieller's argument, E. C. Fieller, Some problems in interval estimation, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 16 (1954), 175-185.

new_concepts.reminder: Student's t distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is the law of a standard normal variable over an independent scaled chi variable.

If $Z$ is standard normal and $W$ is independent chi-squared with $
u$ degrees of freedom, then $Z/\sqrt{W/
u}$ has Student's $t$ distribution with $
u$ degrees of freedom.

statement: Let $a$ be a [regular singular point](c:regular-singular-point) of $y'' + \frac{p(x)}{x-a}\,y' + \frac{q(x)}{(x-a)^2}\,y = 0$, with $p, q$ [analytic](c:analytic-function) on $|x - a| < R$. Let $r_1, r_2$ be the roots of the indicial equation $r(r-1) + p(a) r + q(a) = 0$, with $\operatorname{Re} r_1 \ge \operatorname{Re} r_2$. Then the equation has two independent solutions of Frobenius type on $0 < |x - a| < R$.

hypotheses.text: The equation has the form above, so $a$ is a [regular singular point](c:regular-singular-point) and $p, q$ are analytic at $a$.
The power series of $p$ and $q$ at $a$ have [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) at least $R$.

conclusion: There is a solution $y_1 = (x-a)^{r_1} \sum_{n \ge 0} c_n (x-a)^n$ with $c_0 = 1$, and a second solution $(x-a)^{r_2} \sum b_n (x-a)^n$ if $r_1 - r_2 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, or $C y_1 \ln(x-a) + (x-a)^{r_2} \sum b_n (x-a)^n$ if $r_1 - r_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, with $C \ne 0$ when $r_1 = r_2$.

proofs.name: Frobenius series and reduction of order
proofs.slogan: Solve the coefficient recursion at the larger exponent, bound the coefficients to prove convergence, and get the second solution by the same method or by reduction of order.
proofs.scope: The homogeneous equation, with $a = 0$ after a translation. The inhomogeneous equation with analytic right-hand side $g$ is not treated.

roles.why: The form of the equation makes substitution of a series give a recursion with the indicial polynomial as leading factor.
The bound $|p_n|, |q_n| \le M\rho^{-n}$ with $\rho < R$ gives geometric bounds on the coefficients.

steps.slogan: Substitute a [Frobenius series](c:frobenius-method) and read off the indicial polynomial.
steps.detail: Put $a = 0$, $y = \sum_{n \ge 0} c_n x^{r+n}$, $p = \sum p_n x^n$ and $q = \sum q_n x^n$. The coefficient of $x^{r+m}$ gives $I(r+m) c_m = -\sum_{k<m} \bigl((r+k) p_{m-k} + q_{m-k}\bigr) c_k$, with $I(s) = s(s-1) + p_0 s + q_0 = (s - r_1)(s - r_2)$. For $m = 0$ this forces $I(r) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Solve the recursion for the larger exponent $r_1$.
steps.detail: Since $\operatorname{Re} r_1 \ge \operatorname{Re} r_2$, $I(r_1 + m) = m(m + r_1 - r_2) \ne 0$ for $m \ge 1$, and $|I(r_1 + m)| \ge m^2$. So the recursion fixes each $c_m$ from $c_0 = 1$ and gives a formal solution $y_1$.

steps.slogan: Bound the coefficients by a geometric sequence to prove convergence.
steps.detail: Fix $\rho < R$ and $M$ with $|p_n|, |q_n| \le M\rho^{-n}$, and $\rho_1 < \rho$. Let $\theta = \rho_1/\rho$. Induction gives $|c_m| \le K\rho_1^{-m}$, since the right side of the recursion is at most $\frac{M\theta}{1-\theta} \frac{|r_1| + m + 1}{m^2} K \rho_1^{-m}$, which is below $K\rho_1^{-m}$ for large $m$ and $K$ covers small $m$. So the [power series](c:power-series) converges for $|x| < R$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the construction at $r_2$ when $r_1 - r_2$ is not an integer.
steps.detail: If $r_1 - r_2 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, then $I(r_2 + m) = m(m + r_2 - r_1) \ne 0$ and $|I(r_2 + m)| \ge \delta m^2$ for some $\delta > 0$. The same estimate gives $y_2 = x^{r_2} \sum b_n x^n$, independent of $y_1$ because the leading exponents differ.

steps.slogan: Use reduction of order when $r_1 - r_2$ is a nonnegative integer.
steps.detail: Let $N = r_1 - r_2 \ge 0$. Then $y_2 = y_1 \int e^{-\int p/x}\, y_1^{-2}\, dx$ solves the equation, where $e^{-\int p/x} = x^{-p_0} h$ with $h$ analytic and $h(0) = 1$. Since $r_1 + r_2 = 1 - p_0$ the integrand is $x^{-N-1} \sum e_n x^n$ with $e_0 = 1$, so $y_2 = e_N y_1 \ln x + x^{r_2} \sum b_n x^n$. Continuing $y_2$ around $0$ adds a multiple of $y_1$, which the logarithm absorbs, so the series factor converges for $|x| < R$.

steps.slogan: Collect two independent solutions of Frobenius type in each case.
steps.detail: In every case $y_1 \sim x^{r_1}$ while $y_2$ behaves like $x^{r_2}$ or contains $\ln x$, so $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent. Both have Frobenius form on $0 < |x - a| < R$.

concepts.c:regular-singular-point: The singular point has the form that makes the Frobenius series possible.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Analytic coefficients have power series that the recursion uses.
concepts.c:radius-of-convergence: The disc of analyticity of $p$ and $q$ is the disc where the solutions converge.
concepts.c:frobenius-method: The method substitutes a series with a leading power and solves the recursion.
concepts.c:power-series: The coefficients have a geometric bound, so the power series converges.

source.note: The Frobenius method, as in Coddington and Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (McGraw-Hill, 1955), chapter 4.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be quasi-compact quasi-separated [schemes](c:scheme). If the [abelian categories](c:abelian-category) of [quasicoherent sheaves](c:quasicoherent-sheaf) of $X$ and $Y$ are [equivalent](c:equivalence-of-categories), then $X \cong Y$.

hypotheses.text: The [schemes](c:scheme) $X$ and $Y$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
The categories $\mathrm{Qcoh}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Qcoh}(Y)$ are [equivalent](c:equivalence-of-categories) as categories.

proofs.name: Spectrum and center of an abelian category
proofs.slogan: Recover the space of a scheme as a spectrum of its abelian category and the structure sheaf as the center of the local categories.
proofs.scope: An outline of Rosenberg's reconstruction for quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes; steps 1 to 3 rest on the cited work. Gabriel proved the Noetherian case, and Gabber's modification, written by Brandenburg, removes quasi-compactness.

roles.why: Quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness make the comparison map from $X$ to the spectrum a homeomorphism by gluing affine charts.
An equivalence of the categories induces the same structure on the spectra and centers of $X$ and $Y$.

steps.slogan: Define the spectrum of an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) from its structure alone.
steps.detail: Rosenberg attaches to an abelian category $\mathcal{A}$ a topological space $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{A}$ whose points are certain irreducible topologizing subcategories of $\mathcal{A}$ (Gabber's modification in Brandenburg's account). The definition uses no scheme, so an equivalence $\mathcal{A} \simeq \mathcal{B}$ gives a homeomorphism of spectra.

steps.slogan: Compare $X$ with the spectrum of its category of [quasicoherent sheaves](c:quasicoherent-sheaf).
steps.detail: Send a point $x \in X$ to the subcategory of quasi-coherent sheaves supported on the closure of $x$. This map $X \to \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathrm{Qcoh}(X)$ is a homeomorphism: for affine $X = \mathrm{Spec}\,A$ it recovers $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ from $\mathrm{Mod}(A)$, and the general case glues affine charts.

steps.slogan: Attach a local category to each point by localization.
steps.detail: At a point $x$, localize $\mathrm{Qcoh}(X)$ away from sheaves that do not meet $x$. The resulting local category is equivalent to the category of modules over the [local ring](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$.

steps.slogan: Recover the structure sheaf as the center of the local categories.
steps.detail: The center of $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})$, the ring of endomorphisms of its identity functor, is $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$. These centers form a sheaf of local rings on $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathrm{Qcoh}(X)$ that corresponds to $\mathcal{O}_X$ under the homeomorphism.

steps.slogan: Transport everything along the equivalence to get $X \cong Y$.
steps.detail: An equivalence $\mathrm{Qcoh}(X) \simeq \mathrm{Qcoh}(Y)$ gives a homeomorphism of the spectra, compatible with the local categories and their centers. So it gives an isomorphism of locally ringed spaces $(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong (Y, \mathcal{O}_Y)$, which is an isomorphism of schemes.

concepts.c:scheme: The theorem reconstructs a scheme as a locally ringed space.
concepts.c:abelian-category: The spectrum is defined for an abelian category, here sheaves on a scheme.
concepts.c:quasicoherent-sheaf: The category of quasicoherent sheaves is the data that determines the scheme.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The hypothesis is an equivalence, which transports all intrinsic structure.
concepts.c:local-ring: The center of the local category at a point is the local ring there.
